abstract:
The global prevalence of infertility boosts the demands
for assisted
reproduction technology (ART) and medical plasticware for processing
human reproductive cells. The direct exposure risks of these cells
to microplastic (MPs) potentially released from the plasticware, especially
when sperm is extracted by mincing testicular tissues with sharp tools,
remain unknown. Also, there are methodological challenges in confirming
the actual occurrence and visualizing the original morphology of MPs
in the retrieved sperm samples. Here, we identified sub-10-μm
polystyrene (PS) MPs with protein coronas in mechanically retrieved
sperm specimens on PS plastic Petri dishes through optical photothermal
infrared imaging. The particles were mainly generated by the tools
that induced local polymer cutting deformation on the dishes, and
a few originated from resin particles remaining on the dishes during
manufacture. Each 5 mm scratch by the tools could produce 2.0–13
MPs (1.9–560 μm), depending on the extent of surface
damage to the dishes. Most of the MPs (41.7–81.5%) derived
from scratching could be retrieved along with sperm cells, with an
estimated exposure dose of 100–22,000 particles/mL. We offered
reliable evidence of direct human sperm exposure to MPs and advocate
limiting plasticware use to reduce early life health risks for ART-conceived
babies.

Materials and Methods
2.1
PS Petri Dishes and Sperm Specimens
The waste PS Petri dishes (35 mm diameter and 10 mm height; Corning
Falcon, USA) or waste testicular sperm specimens previously used for
or prepared by the mechanical processing of testicular tissues (schematic
in
Figure
a) were
characterized by O-PTIR imaging (
Section
). The testicular tissues obtained from
patients with nonobstructive azoospermia were processed using either
bent or straight 25-GA needles connected to 1 mL tuberculin syringes
[Becton Dickinson Medical (S) Pte. Ltd., USA]. Before analysis, the
waste dishes were air-dried and the waste sperm specimens were dispersed
in deionized (DI) water (18.2 MΩ·cm, 25 °C) and filtered
through 20 nm Al
2
O
3
membranes (25 mm diameter,
AnodiscTM; Whatman, UK). The protocol for analyzing the waste dishes
and sperm specimens was independently reviewed and approved by the
Research Ethics Committee of Shanghai General Hospital in China (20240806031545000).
New PS Petri dishes and needled-syringes from the same manufactures
were used for scratch tests, the packaging remained unopened until
the scratch tests began. The procedures of testicular tissue processing,
scratching, filtering, and air-drying were carried out in an ISO 5
(Class 100) laminar flow cabinet (≥1 μm: 832 particles/m
3
) to minimize airborne particulate contamination.

Scratch-induced
damage to PS Petri dishes upon mechanical sperm
retrieval. (a) Simplified procedures of ICSI using testicular sperm
retrieved by syringe needles, during which the Petri dishes and the
excessive sperm were discarded and used in this study. The procedures
comprise washing and mechanically processing testicular tissues on
new Petri dishes for spermatozoa release, centrifuging and collecting
sperm cells from the resulting pellet, followed by injecting a single
spermatozoon into the oocyte cytoplasm. Two needled-tuberculin syringes
were used for testicular tissue processing, with one serving to stabilize

them. The needles were bent parallel to the base of the dish (tool
#1, bent needles) or were directly utilized with the cutting surface
facing downward (tool #2, straight needles). (b) Photographs of representative
waste PS Petri dishes, showing the stress-whitening effect caused
by scratching with the bent or straight needles. (c) Optical images
of scratches, particles, and sperm cells on the inner bottom surfaces
of the waste dishes. Inset: magnified images of the boxed regions.
2.2
Scratch Tests with or without Culture Medium
In the absence of culture medium, scratch experiments were conducted
to visually observe the physical damage and MP generation on PS Petri
dishes resulting from repeated contact with tools #1–#4 (schematic
in
Figure
a). Briefly,
a syringe [or a glass slide (76.2 × 25.4 × 1 mm
3
; Sail Brand, China)] was held to allow the needle (or the short
side edge) to contact with the surface of a dish lid, gently sliding
horizontally from left to right for 100 repetitions. The included
angle between the tool and the dish base was ∼60°. The
needle was either used as received (with the cutting surface facing
down or up) or after being bent parallel to the base of the dish.
The dish lids before and after scratching and the composition of particles
present on their surfaces were characterized using O-PTIR imaging
(
Section
). Another
group of scratch experiments (
Figure
a) were performed by applying 50 μL of culture
medium [containing human serum albumin (HSA) and gentamicin; Vitrolife,
Sweden] on the inner bottom surfaces of the dishes using the same
procedures as described above to quantitively evaluate the release
of MPs from the dishes into the medium and their retention in the
resulting pellet after centrifugation. Additional dishes were scratched
for 10, 50, 200, or 500 repetitions using tools #2 or #3 to explore
the influence of the scratch number and the orientation of the needle
cutting surface on the release of MPs. The number of scratches is
determined by the surgeon’s experience. Sperm retrieval typically
takes 1 to 10 min, depending on tissue volume. Assuming 10 or 50 scrapes
per minute (considering surgeon variability), the total number of
scrapes ranges from 10 to 500. Also, three dishes without any scratching
were treated in the same manner as the scratched dishes to evaluate
the extractable MPs from their original surfaces.

of MP formation on scratched PS Petri dishes.
(a) Schematic of the experimental setup. The surfaces of new Petri
dishes were scratched using needled syringes or glass slides (tools
#1–#4). A syringe or slide was positioned at a 60° angle
to the base of a dish and moved horizontally 2–4 mm for 100
times. The scratches and particles on the surfaces of the dishes were
characterized by O-PTIR imaging. (b) Optical images of the same area

2.3
Extraction of MPs from the Scratched Surfaces
of the Petri Dishes
After scratching a certain number of
times on the dish, the medium at the scratched area was carefully
aspirated and replaced with 50 μL of fresh medium. This rinsing
process was repeated three times to ensure thorough extraction of
MPs. The medium collected from the dish was combined and mixed with
fresh medium to 250 μL in a 1.5 mL polypropylene centrifuge
tube (Biosharp; Labgic Technology Co., Ltd., China). The mixture was
then centrifuged under conditions (500 × g, 10 min) similar to
those for collecting testicular sperm in the WHO manual.
The resulting supernatant (150 μL) and
pellet (100 μL) were rinsed separately with DI water for microscopic
imaging using our custom-made LSM system (details in
Section 3
of the SI). This instrument can simultaneously image
∼3 μm MPs deposited on a 10 × 10 mm
2
chip,
benefiting from its wide field-of-view submicron-pixel imaging sensors
(∼0.5 μm/pixel) and short sample-to-chip distance (∼5
μm).
The sum of the number of MPs
in the supernatant (N
S
) or pellet (N
P
) corresponded
to total number (TN) of MPs released from the dish. The potential
exposure dosage of MPs to sperm cells (particles/mL) was calculated
by dividing N
P
by the final volume (0.5 mL) of the medium
used to suspend sperm, as recommended by the WHO manual.
For the chemical characterization of MPs
released into the medium, a 50 μL aliquot of a pellet sample
from the dish scratched by tool #2 was vacuum-filtered through an
Al
2
O
3
membrane and then air-dried in a glass
Petri dish (experimental setup in
Figure
a). Subsequently, MPs retained on the membrane
were identified using O-PTIR imaging (
Section
). To discriminate the impact of the medium
on the surface composition of MPs, DI water was adopted as a surrogate
for the medium to replicate scratch and extraction experiments using
the same procedures, with the exception of drying the pellet subsample
on a silicon wafer (12.5 × 12.5 mm
2
, Pelcotec SFG12;
Ted Pella, Inc., USA) with a grid size of 1 × 1 mm
2
.
2.4
O-PTIR Imaging
The same areas on
the dishes before and after scratching and the MPs present on or released
from the dishes were characterized using the O-PTIR microspectroscope
(mIRage, Photothermal Spectroscopy Corp., USA) coupled with reflective
objectives (40×/0.78 NA and 10×/0.30 NA). Before scratching,
squares (5 × 5 mm
2
) were delineated on the dish lids
using a waterproof pen. Optical images of individual squares were
promptly taken and stitched together. Following scratching by the
tools, the squares were reimaged for comparison. The raw O-PTIR spectra
were randomly acquired from the surfaces of the dish lids or the MPs
in reflection mode from 1798 to 950 cm
–1
. The visible-laser
and O-PTIR images (at 1494 or 1658 cm
–1
) of cells
and MPs, with a resolution of 100 or 200 nm/point, were taken at a
rate of 10 or 100 μm/s, a visible-laser power of 5%, an IR power
of 8%, and a detector gain of 2×. The raw O-PTIR spectra were
normalized and the overlaid O-PTIR images were produced using PTIR
Studio software (version 4.3.7471; Photothermal Spectroscopy Corp.,
USA).
2.5
Statistical Analysis
The N
S
, N
P
, TN, and size distribution of MPs released from the
dishes scratched by different tools were compared using a one-way
analysis of variance followed by a Tukey’s test. The statistical
significance was determined for
p
values less than
0.05. The statistical analyses were performed using SPSS Statistics
software (version 17.0; IBM, UK). Data are presented as the mean ±
standard deviation calculated from three replicate samples, unless
otherwise specified.

Supplementary Material
body:
1
Introduction
The exposure and effects
of widespread microplastics (MPs) on human
health have become a pressing concern.
−
Plastic consumer products generate MPs during
normal use, releasing them into the environment and thereby elevating
their human exposure risks.
−
The influx of plastic medical
ware can lead to human exposure to MPs (e.g., via infusion therapy),
,
a critical issue that remains underexplored to date. Assisted reproductive
technology (ART) is a vital treatment for infertility, enabling the
birth of over 10 million babies globally (
Figure
).
Most (∼73%)
of all ART treatments (∼4 million cycles yearly worldwide)
were carried out via intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI).
,
The global demands for ART and related plasticware are ongoing in
the context of infertility prevalence and declining fertility rates
[
Figure S1
of the Supporting Information
(SI)].
,
Polystyrene (PS) is widely used for producing
disposable medical ware (e.g., Petri dishes) due to its perceived
biocompatibility. However, growing evidence reveals that PS MPs can
cause reproductive toxicity and transgenerational effects in laboratory
animals through ingestion or direct interaction with sperm cells.
−
This emphasizes the need to identify MP exposure risk when handling
human reproductive cells using PS plastic Petri dishes.
1
Schematic of
MP exposure routes in the early lives of babies conceived
through ART. Since 1978, ART has led to the birth of over 10 million
babies worldwide. ICSI and conventional in vitro fertilization (IVF)
are the main ARTs for overcoming severe male and nonmale factor infertility
to achieve parenthood, accounting for 73 and 23% of all ART cycles,
respectively. ICSI involves injecting a single spermatozoon into an
oocyte cytoplasm using a glass micropipette, while IVF allows the
male gamete fertilizing the oocyte naturally. Sperm retrieval is often
conducted by mechanically mincing testicular tissues with rigid tools
(such as syringe needles) on plastic Petri dishes. However, during
this process, the potential formation and release of MPs when the
tools scratch the dish surface are overlooked by surgeons. Although
the effects of direct sperm exposure on the early life health of the
conceived babies are unknown, contamination by reproductively toxic
MPs should be avoided. The use of plasticware is increasing along
with the rising demand for ART, and more attention should be paid
to MP contamination of human reproductive cells.
ICSI with testicular sperm offers the possibility
of parenthood
for couples with severe male infertility.
Testicular sperm retrieval involves processing seminiferous tubules
in the culture medium on plastic Petri dishes to release sperm, centrifuging
homogenates, and resuspending the resulting pellet to collect sperm.
The tissues can be stripped using bent needles
(tool #1) attached to tuberculin syringes as recommended by the World
Health Organization (WHO),
ground with
straight needles (with the cutting surface facing down or up, tool
#2 or #3), or minced with glass slides (tool #4) as preferred by different
laboratories.
,
These mechanical methods are
adopted because of their high efficiency in disrupting the tubular
structure and releasing sperm within a few minutes. However, the use
of sharp tools causes multiple scratches on the dish surface (ranging
from tens to hundreds of times depending on the tissue quantity),
potentially leading to MP generation, analogous to the cutting process
observed on chopping boards.
We observed
MP formation on the scratched dish surface under the similar normal
force and sliding speed (1.0 N and 1 mm/s, respectively) as those
applied by surgeons when processing the tissues mechanically (
Figure S2
; details in
Section 1
of the SI). Whether and to what extent MPs could migrate
from the scratched dishes along with the extracted sperm cells remain
unknown. Given the fragility of infertile men’s sperm,
the exposure risk to MPs should be evaluated,
as it is crucial for the early life health of the conceived babies
(
Figure
).
Human
fluid samples are routinely pretreated with chemical reagents
and examined by infrared spectroscopy for MP analysis.
−
However, the MP-contaminated reagents
will interfere with the differentiation of internal MPs in the samples,
especially those of very low abundance. Some reagents (H
2
O
2
and KOH) may also decompose MPs
and thus destroy their original morphology. Additionally,
organic matters will hamper the identification of MPs by infrared
spectroscopy with low spatial resolution and sensitivity.
,
Hence, directly using mechanically retrieved sperm specimens for
infrared analysis without digestion pretreatment should be a reliable
manner to ascertain contamination. However, this can only be accomplished
through high-resolution chemical characterization techniques. Optical
photothermal infrared (O-PTIR) microspectroscopy employs a visible-laser
probe to detect the photothermal response of the sample surface caused
by mid-IR absorption.
We have employed
this novel chemical imaging technique to identify submicron plastics
and physiochemical modification of polymers.
−
O-PTIR holds
promise in directly detecting MPs in the biological matrix but has
not yet been applied in practice.
Here, we first examined PS
Petri dishes and sperm specimens discarded
from the routine testicular sperm retrieval by mechanical methods
with O-PTIR, to explore if mechanical retrieval causes sperm contamination
by MPs and reveal the surface morphology of MPs interacting with the
sperm. Then, we simulated sperm retrieval and compared the number
of MPs released from new PS Petri dishes during scratching with different
tools (#1–#4) using lensless shadow microscopy (LSM),
to estimate the extent of MP contamination during
sperm processing. We further related MP release to the degree of surface
damage caused by different scratching manners to clarify the factors
controlling the release of MPs from the dishes and offer suggestions
for clinic practice for the safety of ICSI.

3
Results and Discussion
3.1
Formation of MPs on PS Petri Dishes during
Mechanical Sperm Retrieval
The cutting deformation of polymer
occurred in local regions of waste PS Petri dishes that were previously
used for processing testicular tissues with bent or straight needles
(tool #1 or #2) (
Figure
a). From optical images of the inner bottom surfaces of the waste
dishes, the scratched areas appeared white in contrast to the transparent
undisturbed areas (
Figure
b), due to stress-whitening caused by the change in local
light propagation. Because the shape and texture of the indenter and
the diverse indenter-dish contact modes are dissimilar, the scratches
formed on the waste dishes (
Figure
c) differed in morphology from those created by the
scratch tester (
Figure S2a
). The straight
needles generated much more and deeper scratches on the waste dishes
than the bent needles, as they processed more tissues and contacted
more frequently with the dish surfaces with sharp tips. The different
extent of scratch damage to the dishes resulting from various tools
might affect the release of MPs (as discussed below). A few particles
along with sperm cells were also noticed in addition to the intertwined
scratches. However, in situ identification of these particles on the
inner bottom surfaces of the dishes was unfeasible due to the dimensional
constraint of the O-PTIR microspectroscope (the height of the dish
bottom exceeded the 40× objective-to-stage distance).
We
simulated the mechanical processing of testicular tissues to observe
the formation of MPs on new PS Petri dishes with the lids instead
of the bottoms in the absence of the tissues and culture medium (
Figure
a). The surface morphologies
of the same areas on the dish lids before and after scratching by
a bent or straight needle (tool #1 or #2), as well as the composition
of particles present on their surfaces, were characterized using O-PTIR
imaging. Before scratching, a few particles composed of PS (
Figure
b, regions S1 and
S2;
Figure
c, points
1–3) were identified on the unscratched areas. After 100 times
of scratching by the bent or straight needle, mars or grooves appeared
on the same areas (
Figure
b, regions S5 and S6). These scratches were uniform in direction
because of the horizontal movement of the needle from left to right
and thus highly distinct in morphologies from the disorderly scratches
on the waste dishes. Meanwhile, numerous PS MPs emerged around the
scratches (
Figure
c, points 6 and 7). The dish lids were partially covered during scratching
or were closed when being transferred to the microspectroscope to
minimize the contamination from airborne particulates. The MPs detected
on the unscratched areas were probably PS resin granules remaining
from the injection molding process. The additional PS MPs in the same
areas could originate from the fracture, scraping, and removal of
local polymer by the needle. Notedly, the number of MPs on the dish
lids scratched in the absence of culture medium was greater than that
of the particles on the waste dishes scratched with the medium (
Figure
c). This indicated
that the waste dishes (before being abandoned) also produced MPs upon
repeated contact with the needles, but the particles have been transferred
along with the sperm cells.
3.2
Occurrence of Protein-MP Complexes in Mechanically
Retrieved Sperm Specimens
We detected PS MPs in waste sperm
specimens that were formerly extracted by processing testicular tissues
with straight needles on the dishes (
Figure
a). The sperm specimens were not subjected
to the digestion and density separation procedures commonly used for
extracting MPs from human fluid samples to eliminate potential contamination
from chemical reagents.
−
Instead, they were characterized by O-PTIR imaging
after being dispersed in DI water, filtered through Al
2
O
3
membranes, and air-dried in capped glass Petri dishes.
As shown in
Figure
a, the surfaces of the membranes were covered with mixtures of spermatozoa,
nongerm cells, and various particles. The integrity of cell morphology
suggested that the nondestructive sample preparation method could
preserve the initial morphology of MPs (if any) to the greatest extent.
By acquiring the O-PTIR spectra and images of the particles around
the cells, we identified PS MPs (6.4–41 μm) with protein
coronas. Unlike the cells and other particles (
Figure
b, points 1–3), the O-PTIR spectra
of the MPs (
Figure
b, points 4–6) displayed the characteristic IR absorption
bands of both PS polymer (the C=C stretching vibrations of benzene
ring at 1602, 1584, 1494, and 1452 cm
–1
and the
=C–H in-plane deformation vibration of ring hydrogens at 1070
and 1030 cm
–1
)
and
proteins (the C=O stretching vibration at ∼1660 cm
–1
and the NH in-plane bending and the C–N stretching vibrations
at ∼1550 cm
–1
).
,
The overlaid O-PTIR images (at 1658 and 1494 cm
–1
) revealed that the IR absorption signals of proteins were perceived
over the entire surfaces of the MPs, rather than being concentrated
as they were on the sperm head or the cell membrane (
Figure
c, regions S1–S3). Human
spermatozoa contain thousands of proteins
that cannot be distinguished from those associated with MPs using
IR spectroscopy. Following incubation with sperm culture medium, we
found that the proteins adsorbed onto MPs primarily originated from
HSA present in the medium (as discussed below). Although searching
for MPs in the complex biological matrix resembles “seeking
a needle in a haystack,” it is the most reliable approach to
verify the presence of MPs and visualize their original morphology
in sperm specimens. For this reason, detecting MPs in sperm samples
retrieved from slightly scratched plastic Petri dishes becomes challenging
due to their low abundance and increased interference from the biological
matrix. Notedly, recovered sperm may intrinsically carry with MPs,
making it unfeasible to distinguish their origin without appropriate
controls and additional mass spectrometry analysis. While dividing
a patient’s testicular tissue into two parts and processing
them on glass and plastic dishes could ideally address background
interference, this approach is not clinically feasible under current
conditions.

Estimation of the Extent of Sperm Contamination
by MPs
The greater the number of MPs released from the scratched
dishes into the medium, the more MPs ultimately remained in the resulting
pellet (sperm cells) after centrifugation. Centrifugation is necessary
for concentrating sperm cells retrieved from the processed testicular
tissues. We further analyzed the MPs in the pellet to estimate the
potential level of MP contamination of the sperm (
Figure
a). As shown in
Figure
b, MPs were observed in projection
images of the dried supernatant and pellet derived from 100 times
of scratching by the four tools. The MPs formed due to scratching
by tool #1 were prone to suspend in the supernatant (58.3% ±
7.7%), whereas those produced by scratching with tools #2, #3, and
#4 were mainly retained in the pellet (65.4% ± 12.4%, 77.8% ±
4.8%, and 81.5% ± 0.30%, respectively) (
Figure
d). Correspondingly, the number of MPs in
the pellet (N
P
) was 3.9–6.3 times higher when 100
scratches were performed with tool #4 (1025 ± 132 particles)
than with tools #1, #2, and #3 (218 ± 15, 163 ± 58, and
260 ± 62 particles, respectively). Moreover, the N
P
of MPs increased by 2–3 orders of magnitude to 9790 ±
686 and 12,275 ± 2421 particles (average: 11,032 particles) when
scratching with tools #2 and #3 for 500 times, as opposed to the counts
of 28 ± 10 and 73 ± 12 particles (average: 50 particles)
determined from 10 scratches, respectively (
Figure S6
). Thus, mechanical methods causing relatively significant
damage to the dishes (either the tools have a stronger damaging ability
or the tool-dish contact time is longer) would result in more MPs
being retained in the pellet, thereby increasing the probability of
MPs-sperm interaction. The pellet will be mixed with 0.5 mL of the
culture medium for resuspending sperm cells before ICSI, as recommended
by WHO.
If mechanical retrieval of testicular
sperm could produce 10–500 scratches on a PS Petri dish each
time, we estimated that the dosage of testicular sperm exposed to
PS MPs might be 100–22,064 particles/mL (i.e., 50 or 11,032
particles/0.5 mL), based on the average N
P
resulting from
10 and 500 scratches made by the needles (50 and 11,032 particles,
respectively). The actual exposure concentration of MPs to sperm cells
may deviate from our estimates, as our analysis only focused on variations
in separation tools and duration. Mechanical sperm retrieval techniques
vary significantly among surgeons, even with standardized protocols.
Differences in tissue separation methods, applied force, and speed
may affect scratch formation and MP generation on plastic Petri dishes.
However, precisely simulating and controlling these factors remains
a challenge in research settings. Future studies should gather additional
sperm samples to assess the actual exposure concentration.

The microsized MPs are visible under inverted

,
and thus unlikely be inadvertently injected into oocytes along with
spermatozoa. However, MPs can attach to sperm cells during in vitro
culture and induce concentration-dependent toxicity.

The observed adverse effect concentrations of MPs (0.1–100

4
Conclusions
Our study demonstrates
the advantage of O-PTIR imaging for identifying
MPs in human sperm samples without requiring destructive pretreatment.
This technique also helps us to reveal that mechanical sperm retrieval
on plastic Petri dishes generates MPs, leading to sperm contamination
and potential prefertilization exposure risks. For men with nonobstructive
azoospermia, a disorder associated with spermatogenic dysfunction,
testicular sperm retrieval combined with ICSI often represents the
only viable option for biological fatherhood.
Therefore, processing testicular sperm must be conducted with meticulous
care to prevent contamination that could compromise fertilization
potential.
Our findings identify a previously
overlooked source of MP contamination in human reproductive cells
and highlight the necessity for further toxicity assessment. Should
MPs released from plastic Petri dishes exert adverse effects, modifying
clinical protocols for mechanical sperm retrieval to integrate safer
practices, such as using syringe needles instead of glass slides and
substituting plastic Petri dishes with scratch-resistant glass alternatives,
would be essential for enhancing ICSI safety. Beyond ICSI procedural
risks, other sources of MP exposure merit systematic evaluation across
the entire workflow of ART. During this process, various types of
plasticware are used for the separation and culture of human reproductive
cells, which may introduce contamination risks.
